notes.wange: Mera for one thing, mega for many: buk mera, buke mega.
notes.jjajja: Kwaro is a grandparent or ancestor; a grandmother is often called adaa.
notes.omusomesa: From pwonyo, to teach. A student is lakwan, from kwano, to read.
notes.kaka: A woman’s brother. Between brothers, people say omera.

guidebook.intro: Acholi nouns have no class prefixes. Plurals are learnt word by word, and “my” changes only for one thing or many.

tips.title: Plurals you learn by heart
body: Many plurals change the end or the vowel of the word: **latin, lutino** (child, children); **laco, coo** (man, men); **dako, mon** (woman, women). Words for people who do something start with **la-** and make the plural with **lu-**: **lapwony, lupwony** (teacher, teachers).

tips.title: A- for I, i- for you
body: Verbs take the person at the front: **a-** for I, **i-** for you, **wa-** for we, **wu-** for you all, **gi-** for they. **Acamo** (I eat), **Amato** (I drink), **Imito ngo?** (what do you want?).
My, your and his come after the noun: **buk mera** (my book), **buke mega** (my books), **buk meri** (your book), **buk mere** (his or her book).

culture.title: Family is wide
body: Your father’s brothers are also your fathers and your mother’s sisters your mothers. **Omin** is a woman’s brother and **lamin** a man’s sister, and cousins are called brothers and sisters too.
